content: Freckles are small, pigmented spots that appear on the skin or mucous membranes, primarily in individuals with fair complexions, where they are more visible. The presence of freckles is determined by genetics and is associated with a variant of the melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) gene, which is a dominant trait. When ultraviolet (UV) rays penetrate the skin, they stimulate melanocytes, the cells responsible for melanin production, leading to the darkening and increased visibility of freckles. However, the distribution of melanin in freckles is uneven. Freckles are often associated with individuals who have light-colored hair, such as blonde or red hair, and are most commonly seen in those with fair or pale skin. They are predominantly found on areas of the skin that are frequently exposed to the sun, such as the face, but can appear on any sun-exposed region. Freckles are uncommon in infants but are more frequently observed in children before puberty. In children, freckles may be temporary and tend to fade as they reach puberty, coinciding with an increase in melanin production. However, in individuals with very fair skin who produce insufficient melanin, freckles may persist into adulthood, indicating a genetic predisposition. Over time, freckles may fade with age in some individuals. It is important to note that freckles are not considered a skin disorder. However, individuals with a genetic tendency to develop freckles may have an increased susceptibility to sunburn and skin cancer. As a result, they should take precautions to protect their skin from UV damage, including the daily application of sunscreen with a minimum sun protection factor (SPF) of 15. Historically, during the Middle Ages and up until the early 15th century in Europe, an abundance of freckles, often referred to as witchmarks or witchspots, was associated with witchcraft. This belief was likely linked to the genetic correlation between freckles and red hair, which was also considered a characteristic of witches. There are two distinct types of freckles: 1. Ephelides: These are flat, light brown or reddish freckles that are genetically determined. They tend to fade during the winter months and are more common in individuals with light skin tones. The appearance of ephelides can be minimized with consistent use of sunscreen. 2. Liver spots (also known as sun spots or lentigines): These are freckles that do not fade during the winter. Lentigines are more frequently observed in older individuals.
